companyCaseStudy.title: How Netflix Built Open Connect to Serve ~15% of Peak Internet Traffic and Cut Backbone Costs
companyCaseStudy.summary: At peak Netflix has been responsible for roughly 15% of downstream internet traffic in some regions. To keep playback smooth and avoid huge transit bills, Netflix built Open Connect — a purpose-built CDN of appliances, BGP/DNS routing, and smart content placement that shifted the majority of traffic out of backbone links into ISP caches.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

Netflix became a giant of video delivery: hundreds of millions of hours streamed every day, global customers in nearly every country, and traffic patterns that at peak once composed roughly 15% of downstream internet traffic in regions like North America. That scale breaks assumptions: if every viewer pulls bytes from a few origin datacenters, backbone bandwidth and transit bills explode and user startup times suffer.

## Problem

- Scale: tens of millions of concurrent streams during regional primetime windows.
- Cost: paying for massive egress across transit providers and CDNs would be expensive and volatile.
- Quality: viewers expect sub-second start times and uninterrupted playback — every extra hop or congested link increases rebuffering risk.

## Challenge

Netflix needed a way to put video as close to viewers as possible, without handing control of delivery entirely to third-party CDNs and without ballooning operational complexity. They had to: 

- Serve extremely high throughput (many Gbps per POP) with predictable performance.
- Control caching, content placement, and versioning for DRM and different bitrates.
- Route clients to the best copy (ISP cache, IXP, or origin) reliably at global scale.

## Solution: Open Connect (high level)

Netflix designed and deployed Open Connect: a global CDN built from three main ideas:

1. Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) — purpose-built cache servers and racks that Netflix ships to ISP networks and Internet Exchange Points. These appliances hold popular content close to viewers.
2. Smart request routing — a combination of DNS and BGP steering used to send client requests to the nearest/most appropriate OCA or PoP.
3. Content placement & prefetching — analytics driven placement that populates OCAs ahead of demand, plus tiered storage: edge caches, regional POPs, and origin object stores.

### Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[Client (Player)] -->|DNS/BGP| Edge[ISP Open Connect Appliance (OCA)]
  Edge -->|Cache hit| Edge
  Edge -->|Cache miss| Regional[Regional POP]
  Regional --> Origin[(Origin Storage & Encoding)]
  Origin --> Regional
  Edge -.->|Telemetry & Metrics| Atlas[Netflix Monitoring]
```

- Clients use DNS+BGP decisions to land at OCA instances inside ISP networks or nearby IXPs.
- If an OCA has the requested chunks, it serves them directly (single hop). On miss, requests cascade to regional POPs or origin.
- Telemetry feeds content placement algorithms that pre-warm caches for predicted demand.

## Key architectural decisions and why they mattered

- Purpose-built appliances instead of fully outsourcing to CDNs: gave Netflix full control over caching logic (critical for ABR streams with many chunk sizes and DRM-aware delivery). 
- Hybrid routing: DNS for locality, BGP announcements for traffic engineering and failover. BGP lets Netflix influence flow at the ISP peering level to avoid congested transit.
- Predictive placement: rather than only reacting to misses, Netflix uses viewing patterns and regional popularity to prefetch chunks, maximizing hit rate for primetime.
- Telemetry-driven operations: rich, near-real-time metrics (cache hit rates, per-PO P95 latencies, network telemetry) drive automated placement and capacity decisions.

## Results (reported & observable effects)

| Metric | Before (centralized origins / CDN reliance) | After (Open Connect) |
|--------|---------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| Backbone egress as % of traffic | High (majority of bytes) | Reduced dramatically (most traffic stays in ISP/IXP caches) |
| Cache hit rate at edge | ~0% for many flows | Often 80%–95% for popular content (depends on region & title) |
| Median startup latency | 200–500 ms (varied by path) | Typically tens of ms when served from OCA |
| Rebuffering incidents | Higher during regional spikes | Lower due to localized serving and prefetching |
| Transit / CDN spend | High and variable | Significantly lower; saved millions annually by reducing transit egress |

Concrete numbers reported in public Netflix materials and internet measurement studies include that in some regions Netflix traffic represented about 15% of downstream traffic at peak; by moving a large fraction of that into Open Connect caches Netflix avoided most transit-level transit for user video delivery. Edge cache hit rates in many PoPs routinely reach the 80%+ range for top titles, which is what makes most of the savings and latency wins possible.

## Operational practices that made Open Connect work

- Automated deployment and remote management of OCAs so ISPs could accept appliances with minimal ops work.
- Strong telemetry and dashboards to detect content misses and congested links quickly.
- Partnership model with ISPs: Netflix provides appliances and peering guidance; ISPs provide rack space and power. Win-win: ISPs see reduced upstream peering stress and better customer QoE.
- Continual measurement: Netflix runs A/B tests on routing strategies, cache sizing, and prefetch thresholds to tune placement vs storage cost tradeoffs.

## Lessons and tradeoffs

- Building your own CDN is capital intensive but gives control: Netflix accepted appliance ops and logistics to optimize for video delivery patterns.
- Prefetching and predictive placement increase storage and network usage ahead of demand; you gain hit rate at the cost of extra edge storage and occasional wasted prefetch bytes.
- BGP-based routing is powerful but complex; the team invested heavily in operational tooling to avoid creating routing instability.

## Final outcome (story form)

By treating delivery as a first-class engineering problem and owning the CDN layer, Netflix moved the majority of byte delivery out of long-haul transit and into the networks where viewers actually live. The effect: lower latency, fewer stalls, and a much more predictable cost profile. Engineers could push new encodes and ABR ladder changes knowing that the content would be served from caches close to viewers, not from a bottlenecked origin.
keyTakeaways: Putting caches inside ISP networks (OCAs) shifts the majority of heavy video traffic off backbone links, improving latency and cutting transit spend.
A mix of DNS and BGP routing plus telemetry-driven prefetching can drive edge cache hit rates into the 80%–95% range for popular content.
Owning delivery (appliances, routing, placement) is operationally expensive but yields predictable QoE and cost benefits at massive scale.

concept.title: Cache Strategies Unlocked: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back — When to Use Each
concept.summary: Caching reduces latency and database load, but *how* you keep cache and database in sync determines correctness, performance, and complexity. This explains cache-aside, write-through, and write-back with analogies, diagrams, code, and pitfalls so you can pick the right strategy for your service.
concept.explanation:
## WHY it matters

Imagine your database as a factory and the cache as a fast shop next door. If the shop isn't stocked correctly or communicates poorly with the factory, customers get stale or missing items — or the factory gets overwhelmed. Caching strategies solve the tradeoff between *latency*, *throughput*, and *consistency*. Used incorrectly, caching causes stale reads, lost writes, and tricky bugs. Used correctly, it can cut read latency from hundreds of milliseconds to single-digit ms and reduce DB cost dramatically.

### An analogy to make it stick

- Cache-aside: The shop clerk checks the fast shelf first. If the item isn't there, they run to the factory, bring it back, and put it on the shelf for next time. Simple, but the clerk (your app) is responsible for keeping shelf + factory consistent.
- Write-through: Every time the factory makes something, the shop clerk immediately updates the shelf first and the factory is updated in lockstep. The shelf is always fresh at the cost of write latency.
- Write-back: The shop accepts changes and keeps them on the shelf, promising to sync to the factory later. Fast writes, but if the shop burns down before syncing, data is lost.

---

## How they work (sequence diagram)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>App: Read/Write request
  App->>Cache: Read (get key)
  alt Cache Hit
    Cache-->>App: Value
    App-->>Client: Return value
  else Cache Miss (Cache-aside)
    App->>DB: Read
    DB-->>App: Value
    App->>Cache: Populate cache
    App-->>Client: Return value
  end
```

---

## Quick comparison (table)

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| **Cache-aside (lazy load)** | Simple, low write overhead, flexible TTLs | Application must handle cache logic; potential stale reads right after writes | Read-heavy workloads where eventual consistency is acceptable (e.g., product catalog) |
| **Write-through** | Cache always fresh after write; simple read path | Higher write latency, heavier write load on cache | Reads dominate and fresh reads are important (e.g., user sessions) |
| **Write-back (write-behind)** | Fast writes, reduces DB load | Risk of data loss on failure; complex eviction/sync logic | High write throughput with tolerance for small window of inconsistency and strong durability measures (e.g., batch analytics) |

---

## BEFORE / AFTER — example: user profile lookup

| Before (no cache) | After (cache-aside) |
|-------------------|----------------------|
| Every page view hits DB for profile -> 50ms/req, DB CPU high | First view hits DB (slow), subsequent views served from cache -> 1–3ms, DB load ↓ 70% |

---

## Concrete examples & minimal code

### Cache-aside (Node.js + Redis)

```js
// read
async function getUser(id) {
  const cacheKey = `user:${id}`;
  const cached = await redis.get(cacheKey);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const user = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$1', [id]);
  if (user) {
    await redis.set(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(user), 'EX', 300); // TTL 5m
  }
  return user;
}

// write (must invalidate)
async function updateUser(id, changes) {
  await db.query('UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id=$1', [id]);
  await redis.del(`user:${id}`); // invalidate so next read repopulates
}
```

Notes: the app handles misses and invalidation. If you don't delete the cache after write, clients may see stale data.

### Write-through (pseudo)

```py
# write-through pseudocode
def update_user(id, data):
    cache.set(f'user:{id}', serialize(data))
    db.update('users', id, data)  # do both synchronously (or behind a reliable queue)
```

Notes: Ensure ordering — prefer writing cache first if reads must see newest value immediately. Consider writing to DB via a durable queue if DB reliability is the concern.

### Write-back (conceptual)

- App writes to cache and marks it dirty.
- A background worker batches dirty entries and writes them to DB periodically.

Risks: node crash before flush = lost writes. Requires persistence of the dirty queue or replication.

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

1. **Stale reads / race after write**
   - Problem: Client A writes then reads immediately but sees old value from cache.
   - Mitigation: Invalidate cache on write (cache-aside), or update cache as part of the write (write-through), or implement read-after-write special-case to bypass cache.

2. **Cache stampede (thundering herd)**
   - Problem: Many requests miss and all hit DB at once.
   - Mitigation: use mutex / singleflight / request coalescing, randomize TTLs, or pre-warm/populate cache.

3. **Eviction surprises**
   - Problem: Evicted items cause repeated DB hits.
   - Mitigation: tune cache size/eviction policy; use TTLs; proactively refresh hot keys.

4. **Write amplification / inconsistency under partitions**
   - Problem: Network partition or partial failures cause cache and DB to diverge.
   - Mitigation: prefer write-through for strong read freshness; use durable queues for write-behind; consider versioning (compare-and-swap) when updating.

5. **Loss of writes with write-back**
   - Problem: dirty cache entries lost before persisting to DB.
   - Mitigation: persist dirty queue to disk, use replication, or avoid write-back for critical data.

6. **Cache poisoning / stale TTLs**
   - Problem: wrong data stored for long TTL.
   - Mitigation: validate writes, use shorter TTL for risky keys, tag invalidation events.

---

## When to choose which

- Choose **cache-aside** when: reads >> writes, eventual consistency is fine, and you want simple, robust behavior. It's the default for many services.
- Choose **write-through** when: you need fresh reads immediately after writes and can tolerate extra write latency or cache write failures.
- Choose **write-back** when: you have extremely high write rates, can tolerate a short window of inconsistency, and can guarantee durability of pending writes (rare for business-critical data).

---

## Operational tips

- Monitor cache hit rate, eviction rate, latency, and DB load.
- Implement metrics: e.g., cache_hits, cache_misses, cache_latency, db_queries_per_second.
- Use multi-layer caching: CDN edge cache + in-app Redis + DB.
- Apply TTLs and randomized jitter on TTLs to avoid synchronized expirations.
- Use singleflight libraries (Go) or lock-per-key to prevent stampede.

---

## Summary

Caching is not a silver bullet — it’s a strategy tradeoff between performance and consistency. Understand your read/write patterns, failure modes, and how fresh your reads must be. Start with cache-aside for simplicity; move to write-through or write-behind only when your workload and operational guarantees justify the extra complexity.
keyTakeaways: Cache-aside is simple and safe for read-heavy, eventually-consistent workloads — the app owns cache logic.
Write-through ensures fresh reads but increases write latency and complexity; write-back is fastest for writes but risky without durable buffering.
Prevent stampedes, tune TTLs, and monitor hit/eviction metrics — most caching problems are operational, not theoretical.
